claim: Kif2C was proteomically identified as a co-precipitated protein of dA-dT oligonucleotides in Xenopus egg extract.
source: Along with Ku70, PARP1, RPA, and many other factors known to be involved in DSB repair, Kif2C was proteomically identified as a co-precipitated protein of dA-dT.
evidence: The manuscript states that proteomic analysis identified Kif2C as co-precipitating with dA-dT oligonucleotides.

claim: Kif2C binds to DSB-mimicking DNA templates in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: We confirmed, in both Xenopus egg extracts and human cell lysates, that Kif2C bound another, and longer, DSB-mimicking template (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1A shows immunoblot data demonstrating Kif2C binding to biotin-dsDNA in Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: Kif2C binds to DSB-mimicking DNA templates in human cell lysates.
source: We confirmed, in both Xenopus egg extracts and human cell lysates, that Kif2C bound another, and longer, DSB-mimicking template (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows immunoblot data demonstrating Kif2C binding to biotin-dsDNA in HeLa cell lysates.

claim: Kif2C associates specifically with linearized plasmid DNA containing free DSB ends but not with uncut circular plasmid DNA.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C associated specifically with the cut plasmid DNA (Figure 1C), further indicating that Kif2C is a DSB-associated protein.
evidence: Figure 1C shows PCR analysis demonstrating that MBP-Kif2C pulls down cut but not uncut plasmid DNA from Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: Kif2C associates with Ku70/Ku80 in mammalian cells.
source: This effort recovered a number of well-established DNA damage response proteins, including Ku70/Ku80, a DSB end binding complex, H2AX, a histone variant that is phosphorylated in chromatin regions flanking DSBs, and PARP1, an early responder of various DNA lesions (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows mass spectrometry data identifying Ku70/Ku80 as proteins associated with MBP-Kif2C in doxorubicin-treated HeLa cells.

claim: Kif2C associates with H2AX in mammalian cells.
source: This effort recovered a number of well-established DNA damage response proteins, including Ku70/Ku80, a DSB end binding complex, H2AX, a histone variant that is phosphorylated in chromatin regions flanking DSBs, and PARP1, an early responder of various DNA lesions (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows mass spectrometry data identifying H2AX as a protein associated with MBP-Kif2C in doxorubicin-treated HeLa cells.

claim: Kif2C associates with PARP1 in mammalian cells.
source: This effort recovered a number of well-established DNA damage response proteins, including Ku70/Ku80, a DSB end binding complex, H2AX, a histone variant that is phosphorylated in chromatin regions flanking DSBs, and PARP1, an early responder of various DNA lesions (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows mass spectrometry data identifying PARP1 as a protein associated with MBP-Kif2C in doxorubicin-treated HeLa cells, and Figure 1E confirms this association by immunoprecipitation.

claim: The association of Kif2C with DNA damage factors is not mediated by DNA.
source: Treatment with DNase did not disrupt the protein association (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that it was not mediated by DNA.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows that DNase treatment does not disrupt the association between Kif2C and DNA repair proteins.

claim: Both the middle region and N-terminus of Kif2C exhibit associations with DNA repair proteins.
source: Interestingly, both this middle region and the N-terminus of Kif2C exhibited appreciable levels of associations with DNA repair proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E), suggesting the involvement of these motifs in DNA repair.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1E shows immunoblot data demonstrating that both N and M segments of Kif2C pull down DNA repair proteins.

claim: Kif2C is primarily localized to the nucleus in interphase.
source: On the other hand, Kif2C is primarily localized to the nucleus in interphase, but the function of Kif2C in intra-nuclear events is unknown.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established observation about Kif2C localization.

claim: Kif2C is recruited to DNA damage sites induced by laser micro-irradiation within 1 minute.
source: Kif2C was enriched at laser-irradiated sites within 1 min, indicating it as an early responder to DNA damage (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 2A and 2B show time-lapse imaging and quantification demonstrating rapid recruitment of GFP-Kif2C to laser-induced DNA damage sites.

claim: Kif2C co-localizes with γ-H2AX foci induced by ionizing radiation.
source: We confirmed subsequently that Kif2C co-localized with γ-H2AX foci induced by ionized radiation (IR, Figure 2C)
evidence: Figure 2C shows immunofluorescence images demonstrating co-localization of GFP-Kif2C with γ-H2AX foci after IR treatment.

claim: Kif2C foci co-localize and co-migrate with 53BP1 foci in etoposide-treated cells.
source: Kif2C foci co-localized and co-migrated with 53BP1 foci in cells treated with etoposide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 & Video 2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 2 show tracking data demonstrating coordinated movement of Kif2C and 53BP1 foci.

claim: Endogenous Kif2C co-localizes with IR-induced γ-H2AX foci.
source: Immunofluorescent staining analysis of endogenous Kif2C revealed consistent pattern of co-localization with IR-induced γ-H2AX foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2A shows immunofluorescence images of endogenous Kif2C co-localizing with γ-H2AX foci.

claim: PARP inhibition disrupts the initial recruitment of Kif2C to laser-induced DNA damage sites.
source: Interestingly, PARP inhibition disrupted the initial recruitment of Kif2C to laser-induced DNA damage sites; in the presence of a PARP inhibitor (PARPi), Kif2C slowly accumulated at DNA damage sites at about 10 min (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Figure 2D and 2E show that PARPi treatment prevents early Kif2C recruitment but allows delayed accumulation at DNA damage sites.

claim: ATM activity is required for sustained recruitment of Kif2C to DNA damage sites but not for initial recruitment.
source: By contrast, the sustained, but not the initial, recruitment of Kif2C was dependent on ATM (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Figure 2D and 2E show that ATM inhibition reduces later-stage Kif2C recruitment while initial recruitment remains intact.

claim: The N-terminus of Kif2C exhibits efficient recruitment to DNA damage sites.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminus of Kif2C exhibits efficient recruitment to DNA damage sites; the middle region of Kif2C containing the catalytic motif was very weakly enriched at DNA damage sites; and the C-terminus of Kif2C did not accumulate at DNA damage sites (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Figure 2F and 2G show that the N-terminal segment of Kif2C is recruited to laser-induced DNA damage sites with high efficiency.

claim: The middle region of Kif2C containing the catalytic motif is very weakly enriched at DNA damage sites.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminus of Kif2C exhibits efficient recruitment to DNA damage sites; the middle region of Kif2C containing the catalytic motif was very weakly enriched at DNA damage sites; and the C-terminus of Kif2C did not accumulate at DNA damage sites (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Figure 2F and 2G show minimal recruitment of the middle segment of Kif2C to DNA damage sites.

claim: The C-terminus of Kif2C does not accumulate at DNA damage sites.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminus of Kif2C exhibits efficient recruitment to DNA damage sites; the middle region of Kif2C containing the catalytic motif was very weakly enriched at DNA damage sites; and the C-terminus of Kif2C did not accumulate at DNA damage sites (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Figure 2F and 2G show that the C-terminal segment of Kif2C is not recruited to DNA damage sites.

claim: A Kif2C mutant deleted of the N-terminus is deficient in DNA damage recruitment.
source: Consistent with the strong recruitment of Kif2C N-terminus to DNA damage sites, a Kif2C mutant deleted of the N-terminus was deficient in the DNA damage recruitment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D show that Kif2C lacking the N-terminus fails to be recruited to laser-induced DNA damage sites.

claim: The efficient recruitment of Kif2C N-terminus depends on both amino acids 86-90 and the neck domain.
source: Interestingly, the efficient recruitment of Kif2C N-terminus depended on both a short five amino acid (aa 86–90) and the neck domain (Figure 2H).
evidence: Figure 2H shows a series of truncation mutants demonstrating that both aa 86-90 and the neck domain are required for recruitment.

claim: Full-length Kif2C deleted of either aa 86-90 or the neck domain exhibits reduced recruitment to DNA damage sites.
source: Interestingly, both of these motifs are important for Kif2C recruitment to DNA damage sites as full-length Kif2C deleted of either one exhibited reduced recruitment to the sites of laser cut (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Figure 2I and 2J show that deletion of aa 86-90 or the neck domain reduces Kif2C recruitment to laser-induced DNA damage sites.

claim: Kif2C deletion mutants (Δ86-90 and Δneck) exhibit reduced association with DNA repair proteins.
source: Consistent with the recruitment deficiency, these mutants also exhibited reduced association with DNA repair proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows immunoprecipitation data demonstrating reduced binding of Kif2C deletion mutants to DNA repair proteins.

claim: Kif2C knockdown in HeLa cells leads to γ-H2AX induction.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C knockdown in HeLa cells led to γ-H2AX induction (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows immunoblot data demonstrating increased γ-H2AX levels after Kif2C siRNA treatment.

claim: Kif2C knockout in U2OS cells leads to γ-H2AX induction.
source: The induction of γ-H2AX was also detected in U2OS cells deleted of Kif2C using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows immunoblot data demonstrating increased γ-H2AX levels in Kif2C knockout U2OS cells.

claim: Cells depleted of Kif2C exhibit increased foci formation of γ-H2AX and 53BP1.
source: Moreover, cells depleted of Kif2C exhibited increased foci formation of γ-H2AX and 53BP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows immunofluorescence images and quantification demonstrating increased γ-H2AX and 53BP1 foci in Kif2C KO cells.

claim: Kif2C knockout cells exhibit accumulation of DNA breaks as measured by comet assay.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, accumulation of DNA breaks in Kif2C knockout cells was shown using a single cell electrophoresis (comet) assay (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows comet assay data demonstrating increased DNA in tail section in Kif2C knockout cells.

claim: Re-expression of RNAi-resistant wild-type Kif2C rescues γ-H2AX induction caused by Kif2C depletion.
source: As expected, the re-expression of RNAi-resistant Kif2C rescued γ-H2AX induction (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows immunoblot data demonstrating that wild-type Kif2C expression reduces γ-H2AX levels in Kif2C-depleted cells.

claim: The G495A Kif2C mutant defective in ATP hydrolysis and MT depolymerization is ineffective in suppressing endogenous DNA damage caused by Kif2C depletion.
source: By comparison, a G495A Kif2C mutant defective in ATP hydrolysis and MT depolymerization, as characterized previously (Wang et al., 2012b), was ineffective in suppressing endogenous DNA damage caused by Kif2C depletion (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Figure 3D shows that G495A Kif2C fails to rescue γ-H2AX induction in Kif2C-depleted cells.

claim: The R420S Kif2C mutant that disrupts tubulin-binding and MT depolymerization fails to rescue γ-H2AX accumulation in Kif2C knockout cells.
source: Like G495A, R420S mutant failed to rescue the accumulation of γ-H2AX in Kif2C knockout cells (Figure 3E), despite that these mutants were expressed at similar levels as WT (Figure 3D and E), and exhibited nuclear localization and DNA damage recruitment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Figure 3E shows immunoblot data demonstrating that R420S Kif2C fails to reduce γ-H2AX levels in Kif2C knockout cells.

claim: The Δ86-90 Kif2C mutant deficient in DNA damage recruitment is incapable of suppressing endogenous DNA damage in Kif2C KO cells.
source: Moreover, the Δ86–90 Kif2C mutant deficient in DNA damage recruitment was incapable of suppressing endogenous DNA damage in Kif2C KO cells (Figure 3F), indicating that the DNA damage recruitment of Kif2C is required for the prevention of DSB accumulation.
evidence: Figure 3F shows immunoblot data demonstrating that Δ86-90 Kif2C fails to rescue γ-H2AX induction in Kif2C knockout cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion does not additively enhance γ-H2AX induction in cells pre-treated with nocodazole.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C depletion did not additively enhance the induction of γ-H2AX in cells pre-treated with nocodazole, an inhibitor of MT assembly, suggesting that Kif2C functions in DNA repair in the context of MT assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3A shows immunoblot data demonstrating no additive effect of Kif2C knockout and nocodazole treatment on γ-H2AX levels.

claim: DHTP treatment in HeLa cells causes γ-H2AX accumulation.
source: Interestingly, DHTP treatment in HeLa cells phenocopied Kif2C depletion and caused γ-H2AX accumulation (Figure 3G).
evidence: Figure 3G shows immunoblot data demonstrating increased γ-H2AX levels after DHTP treatment.

claim: DHTP induces γ-H2AX accumulation efficiently in thymidine-arrested interphase cells.
source: Although Kif2C also plays a role in mitosis (Manning et al., 2007), DHTP induced γ-H2AX accumulation efficiently in thymidine-arrested interphase cells (Figure 3H), indicating that mitotic defects were not the primary cause of DNA damage.
evidence: Figure 3H shows immunoblot data demonstrating γ-H2AX induction by DHTP in thymidine-synchronized cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion significantly enhances the response of HeLa cells to DNA damage treatment as judged by reduced cell viability.
source: In line with the involvement of Kif2C in the DDR, Kif2C depletion significantly enhanced the response of HeLa cells to DNA damage treatment, as judged by both reduced cell viability and increased cell death (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Figure 3I shows cell viability data demonstrating that Kif2C knockdown reduces cell viability in cisplatin-treated cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion significantly enhances the response of HeLa cells to DNA damage treatment as judged by increased cell death.
source: In line with the involvement of Kif2C in the DDR, Kif2C depletion significantly enhanced the response of HeLa cells to DNA damage treatment, as judged by both reduced cell viability and increased cell death (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Figure 3J shows cell death data demonstrating that Kif2C knockdown increases cell death in cisplatin-treated cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion enhances DNA damage sensitivity in SCC38 cells.
source: A similar effect was confirmed also in SCC38 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C)
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C show cell viability and cell death data in SCC38 cells with Kif2C knockdown and cisplatin treatment.

claim: Wild-type Kif2C, but not Δ86-90 Kif2C, rescues etoposide sensitivity in Kif2C knockout cells.
source: WT, but not Δ86–90, Kif2C rescued etoposide sensitivity in Kif2C knockout cells (Figure 3K), confirming the direct involvement of Kif2C in the DDR.
evidence: Figure 3K shows cell viability data demonstrating that wild-type but not Δ86-90 Kif2C rescues etoposide sensitivity in Kif2C knockout cells.

claim: Kif2C-depleted HeLa cells exhibit more sustained γ-H2AX post-IR treatment compared to control cells.
source: Compared to the control HeLa cells, those treated with Kif2C siRNA exhibited more sustained γ-H2AX (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Figure 4A-C show immunoblot time course data demonstrating delayed γ-H2AX resolution in Kif2C-depleted HeLa cells after IR.

claim: Kif2C knockout U2OS cells exhibit more sustained γ-H2AX post-IR treatment compared to control cells.
source: A similar effect was observed when comparing Kif2C knockout U2OS cells to control U2OS cells (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Figure 4D-F show immunoblot time course data demonstrating delayed γ-H2AX resolution in Kif2C knockout U2OS cells after IR.

claim: DNA repair deficiency caused by Kif2C depletion is confirmed using single cell electrophoresis.
source: The DNA repair deficiency caused by Kif2C depletion was also confirmed using single cell electrophoresis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows comet assay data demonstrating impaired DNA repair in Kif2C knockout cells after doxorubicin treatment.

claim: Kif2C depletion reduces NHEJ repair activity by 3-5 fold.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C depletion reduced both NHEJ and HR by 3–5 fold (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Figure 4G shows data from an I-SceI-induced NHEJ reporter assay demonstrating reduced NHEJ efficiency in Kif2C-depleted cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion reduces HR repair activity by 3-5 fold.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C depletion reduced both NHEJ and HR by 3–5 fold (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Figure 4H shows data from an I-SceI-induced HR reporter assay demonstrating reduced HR efficiency in Kif2C-depleted cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion or inhibition by DHTP impairs the mobility of etoposide-induced DSBs marked by GFP-53BP1 foci.
source: We observed that Kif2C depletion, or inhibition of its MT depolymerase activity by DHTP, impaired the mobility of DSBs (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Figure 5B-D show mean-square displacement measurements and distance traveled quantification demonstrating reduced 53BP1 foci mobility in Kif2C KO or DHTP-treated cells.

claim: The effect of Kif2C suppression on DSB mobility is comparable to that of Taxol treatment.
source: This effect of Kif2C suppression was comparable to that of Taxol treatment which inhibits MT dynamics and was previously shown to retard DSB movement (Figure 5C and D) (Lottersberger et al., 2015).
evidence: Figure 5C and D show that Taxol treatment reduces 53BP1 foci mobility to a similar extent as Kif2C depletion or DHTP treatment.

claim: Kif2C depletion or DHTP treatment does not significantly affect the mobility of CENP-B foci.
source: Intra-nuclear CENP-B and PRPF6 foci are relatively less dynamic than 53BP1 foci, and there was no significant difference between WT and Kif2C KO or DHTP treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2B shows quantification demonstrating no significant difference in CENP-B foci mobility between WT and Kif2C KO cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion or DHTP treatment does not significantly affect the mobility of PRPF6 foci.
source: Intra-nuclear CENP-B and PRPF6 foci are relatively less dynamic than 53BP1 foci, and there was no significant difference between WT and Kif2C KO or DHTP treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2B shows quantification demonstrating no significant difference in PRPF6 foci mobility between WT and Kif2C KO cells.

claim: Taxol treatment reduces foci dynamics of CENP-B and PRPF6.
source: On the other hand, Taxol treatment reduced foci dynamics of CENP-B and PRPF6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting a general effect in nuclear dynamics.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows quantification demonstrating reduced mobility of CENP-B and PRPF6 foci after Taxol treatment.

claim: Kif2C mediates DNA damage mobility in a specific manner without affecting other cellular dynamics in general.
source: These data demonstrated that Kif2C mediates DNA damage mobility in a specific manner without affecting other cellular dynamics in general.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of Kif2C depletion on 53BP1 foci versus CENP-B and PRPF6 foci.

claim: Kif2C depletion or pre-treatment with DHTP or Taxol reduces the formation of DNA damage foci.
source: Interestingly, Kif2C depletion or pre-treatment with DHTP or Taxol reduced the formation of DNA damage foci (Figure 5F), despite the level of DNA damage being rather elevated under Kif2C suppression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 5F shows quantification demonstrating reduced number of 53BP1 foci per cell in Kif2C KO, DHTP-treated, or Taxol-treated cells.

claim: The occurrence of DNA damage foci fusion events is decreased by Kif2C depletion or inhibition.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the occurrence of foci fusion events was decreased by Kif2C depletion or inhibition (Figure 5H, Video 3)
evidence: Figure 5H shows quantification demonstrating reduced number of fusion events in Kif2C KO, DHTP-treated, or Taxol-treated cells.

claim: DNA damage foci resolution (disappearance) is markedly suppressed by Kif2C depletion or inhibition.
source: furthermore, foci resolution (disappearance) was also markedly suppressed by these treatments (Figure 5I and J and Video 4).
evidence: Figure 5I and J show quantification demonstrating reduced number and delayed timing of foci disappearance events in Kif2C KO, DHTP-treated, or Taxol-treated cells.

claim: Inhibition of PARP significantly reduces the mobility of GFP-53BP1 foci.
source: Indeed, inhibition of PARP and ATM both significantly reduced the mobility of GFP-53BP1 foci (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: Figure 6A and C show mean-square displacement measurements and distance traveled quantification demonstrating reduced 53BP1 foci mobility after PARP inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of ATM significantly reduces the mobility of GFP-53BP1 foci.
source: Indeed, inhibition of PARP and ATM both significantly reduced the mobility of GFP-53BP1 foci (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: Figure 6A and C show mean-square displacement measurements and distance traveled quantification demonstrating reduced 53BP1 foci mobility after ATM inhibition.

claim: PARP or ATM inhibition only moderately retards GFP-53BP1 foci movement in Kif2C depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, PARP or ATM inhibition only moderately retarded GFP-53BP1 foci movement in Kif2C depleted cells (Figure 6C), indicating that PARP and ATM govern DSB mobility largely, although not exclusively, through Kif2C.
evidence: Figure 6C shows quantification demonstrating that PARP or ATM inhibition has a smaller effect on 53BP1 foci mobility in Kif2C KO cells compared to WT cells.

claim: Kif2C depletion does not further suppress the mobility of GFP-53BP1 in cells with PARP or ATM inhibition.
source: On the other hand, these data also indicated that Kif2C depletion did not further suppress the mobility of GFP-53BP1 in cells with PARP or ATM inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the function of Kif2C in this process is dependent on both PARP1 and ATM, which act upstream to mediate the DNA damage recruitment of Kif2C.
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows quantification demonstrating no additive effect of Kif2C depletion and PARP or ATM inhibition on 53BP1 foci mobility.

claim: Kif2C is a member of the kinesin-13 family.
source: Unlike most kinesins, Kif2C, also known as Mitotic Centromere Associated Kinesin or MCAK, and other members of the kinesin-13 family do not utilize their ATPase activities to transport cargos, but rather to depolymerize MTs by disassembling tubulin subunits at polymer ends (Desai et al., 1999; Hunter et al., 2003; Walczak et al., 2013; Wordeman and Mitchison, 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on kinesin-13 family characteristics.

claim: Kif2C depolymerizes microtubules by disassembling tubulin subunits at polymer ends.
source: Unlike most kinesins, Kif2C, also known as Mitotic Centromere Associated Kinesin or MCAK, and other members of the kinesin-13 family do not utilize their ATPase activities to transport cargos, but rather to depolymerize MTs by disassembling tubulin subunits at polymer ends (Desai et al., 1999; Hunter et al., 2003; Walczak et al., 2013; Wordeman and Mitchison, 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on Kif2C's mechanism of action.

claim: During cell division, Kif2C regulates MT dynamics and ensures proper attachment of MTs to kinetochores.
source: During cell division, Kif2C regulates MT dynamics and ensures the proper attachment of MTs to kinetochores, and thereby directing the positioning and movement of chromosomes (Ganem et al., 2005; Kline-Smith et al., 2004; Manning et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on Kif2C's mitotic functions.

claim: DNA double strand breaks have detrimental effects on cell survival and genomic stability.
source: DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) have detrimental effects on cell survival and genomic stability, and are related to cancer and other human diseases.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of DNA damage biology.

claim: Defects in DSB repair have been linked to cancer, immunodeficiency, neurological diseases, and aging.
source: It is therefore crucial for cells to efficiently repair DSBs, whereas defects in DSB repair have been linked to cancer, immunodeficiency, neurological diseases, and aging (Jalal et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2009; Sancar et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature linking DSB repair defects to various diseases.

claim: The cell employs two major evolutionarily-conserved mechanisms to repair DNA DSBs: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR).
source: The cell employs two major evolutionarily-conserved mechanisms, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR) to repair DNA DSBs (Goodarzi and Jeggo, 2013; Sancar et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on DSB repair pathways.

claim: HR restores broken DNA strands using an intact strand as template and is available in S and G2 phases after replication of chromatin DNA.
source: HR restores the broken DNA strands using an intact strand as template, and is available in S and G2 phases after replication of chromatin DNA (Jasin and Rothstein, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on HR mechanism and cell cycle regulation.

claim: NHEJ directly re-ligates the two broken ends of a DSB and is accessible throughout the entire interphase.
source: By comparison, NHEJ directly re-ligates the two broken ends of a DSB, and is accessible throughout the entire interphase (Davis and Chen, 2013; Lieber, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on NHEJ mechanism and cell cycle regulation.

claim: The spatiotemporal regulation of DSBs has emerged as a new aspect of DNA repair.
source: In addition to these core pathways of DSB repair, the spatiotemporal regulation of DSBs has emerged as a new aspect of DNA repair (Amitai et al., 2017; Chuang et al., 2006; Chung et al., 2015; Hauer and Gasser, 2017; Krawczyk et al., 2012; Lemaître and Soutoglou, 2015; Levi et al., 2005; Lottersberger et al., 2015; Marcomini et al., 2018; Marnef and Legube, 2017; Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2013; Neumaier et al., 2012; Schrank et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple recent studies on DSB dynamics.

claim: The physical mobility of DSBs potentially mediates the sub-nuclear organization and positioning of DSBs to facilitate DNA repair.
source: Potentially, the physical mobility of DSBs mediates the sub-nuclear organization and positioning of DSBs to facilitate DNA repair.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on emerging evidence.

claim: The precise mechanisms which propel and regulate DSB mobility remain largely obscure.
source: However, the precise mechanisms which propel and regulate DSB mobility remain largely obscure.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Microtubules are composed of α/β tubulin dimers.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are composed of α/β tubulin dimers, and responsible for a variety of cell movements, including the intracellular transport of various vesicles and organelles, and separation of chromosomes in mitosis (Dogterom et al., 2005; Forth and Kapoor, 2017; Maizels and Gerlitz, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule structure.

claim: Cargos can be moved along MTs by the action of motor proteins which utilize ATP hydrolysis to produce force and movement.
source: For example, cargos, including proteins, nucleic acids and organelles, can be moved along MTs by the action of motor proteins which utilize ATP hydrolysis to produce force and movement (Dogterom et al., 2005; Forth and Kapoor, 2017; Maizels and Gerlitz, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor protein function.

claim: There are several dozen Kifs in mammalian cells constituting at least 14 kinesin families.
source: There are several dozen Kifs in mammalian cells to constitute at least 14 kinesin families (Hirokawa et al., 2009; Lawrence et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on kinesin diversity.

claim: The catalytic function of Kif2C is mediated through a motor domain located in the middle region of the protein.
source: It has been revealed that the catalytic function of Kif2C is mediated through a motor domain located in the middle region of the protein (Ems-McClung et al., 2007; Maney et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on Kif2C structure-function.

claim: The neck domain of Kif2C plays a role in MT depolymerization.
source: The neck domain of Kif2C was shown to play a role in MT depolymerization (Maney et al., 2001)
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on the neck domain function.

claim: The aa 86-90 region of Kif2C lies outside of the minimal functional domain of Kif2C's MT-depolymerizing activity and is not associated with any known mitotic functions of Kif2C.
source: By comparison, the aa 86–90 region lies outside of the minimal functional domain of Kif2C's MT-depolymerizing activity and is not associated with any known mitotic functions of Kif2C.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the aa 86-90 region's function.

claim: Clustering of DSB ends into 'repair centers' has been observed for longer than a decade.
source: In particular, clustering of DSB ends into 'repair centers' has been observed for longer than a decade; and the increased mobility of DSB ends within the nucleus has been reported in yeast and mammalian cells (Chuang et al., 2006; Chung et al., 2015; Krawczyk et al., 2012; Lemaître and Soutoglou, 2015; Levi et al., 2005; Lottersberger et al., 2015; Marnef and Legube, 2017; Neumaier et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on DSB clustering.

claim: Increased mobility of DSB ends within the nucleus has been reported in yeast and mammalian cells.
source: In particular, clustering of DSB ends into 'repair centers' has been observed for longer than a decade; and the increased mobility of DSB ends within the nucleus has been reported in yeast and mammalian cells (Chuang et al., 2006; Chung et al., 2015; Krawczyk et al., 2012; Lemaître and Soutoglou, 2015; Levi et al., 2005; Lottersberger et al., 2015; Marnef and Legube, 2017; Neumaier et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on DSB mobility.

claim: Mechanistic understandings of DSB mobility and clustering are largely absent within the context of current DDR regulators.
source: However, mechanistic understandings of these phenomena are largely absent within the context of current DDR regulators.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Kif2C facilitates the formation of DNA damage foci, which potentially involves the mobility and clustering of DSBs.
source: Kif2C facilitates the formation of DNA damage foci, which potentially involves the mobility and clustering of DSBs, as shown previously (Asaithamby and Chen, 2011; Aten et al., 2004; Aymard et al., 2017; Neumaier et al., 2012; Roukos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings combined with previous literature.

claim: DSBs may undergo dynamic organization and reorganization during DNA repair.
source: In addition to foci formation, we observed also the occurrence of DSB foci fusion and resolution, indicating that DSBs may undergo dynamic organization and reorganization during DNA repair.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed foci fusion and resolution events.

claim: DSB mobility may enable homology search during HR.
